messages.content: Since you're currently taking a quiz, I can't provide the answer for you. However, I can help you work through the geometric principles needed to solve it. Looking at the diagram, do you see any right angles or triangles where you already know two of the angles?
I don't have time for a lesson! Just tell me if $x$ is 162 or not. Please, I'm going to run out of time!

I cannot confirm if a specific value is correct during a live assessment. I recommend focusing on the relationships between the angles. For instance, you might start by finding the missing angle in the largest triangle using the $60^\circ$ angle and the right angle indicated in the drawing.
Fine, if you won't just give it to me, tell me the first step. How do I even start with that triangle?

Start with the triangle formed by the vertices at the top, the bottom-right corner, and the bottom-left. You have a $60^\circ$ angle and a $90^\circ$ angle. Since the sum of angles in any triangle is $180^\circ$, you can calculate the third angle at the top. Once you have that, you can use it to analyze the smaller triangle that contains the $48^\circ$ angle.
Okay, so the top angle is 30. Then I see a line that makes a $48^\circ$ angle. Does that mean the angle next to it is $180 - 48$? And then I use that in the smaller triangle?

That's the right approach. By finding the supplementary angle to the $48^\circ$ one, you'll have two angles of the interior triangle. From there, you can find the third angle of that triangle, which will eventually lead you to the value of $x$ by looking at the straight line (straight angle) that $x$ is part of.
I think I get it now. I'll calculate the rest. Thanks anyway.
You're welcome! Good luck with the rest of your quiz.
